putnam-2015-a1.title: Normalize by an area-preserving map
putnam-2015-a1.body:
**Setup.** The map $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$ preserves the hyperbola and all areas, so we may assume both points lie on the branch in the first quadrant: $A=(t_1,1/t_1)$, $B=(t_2,1/t_2)$ with $0<t_1<t_2$. Points between them are $(t,1/t)$ with $t_1<t<t_2$.

**Area-preserving symmetries.** For $\lambda>0$ the linear map $\phi_\lambda(x,y) = (\lambda x, y/\lambda)$ has determinant $1$, so it preserves areas; it maps the hyperbola $xy=1$ onto itself, maps chords to chords, and preserves the order of points along the branch. Hence it carries triangles $APB$ to triangles $A'P'B'$ of the same area, and the regions between the hyperbola and a chord to the corresponding regions. So both the hypothesis and the conclusion are unchanged if we replace $A,B,P$ by their images.

Choose $\lambda = 1/\sqrt{t_1t_2}$. Then $A' = (s, 1/s)$ and $B' = (1/s, s)$ with $s = \sqrt{t_1/t_2} < 1$; these two points are mirror images in the line $y=x$.

**Locating $P$.** The chord $A'B'$ lies on the line $x+y = s + 1/s$. For $Q=(t,1/t)$ with $s<t<1/s$, the distance from $Q$ to this line is
$$\frac{(s+1/s) - (t+1/t)}{\sqrt 2},$$
which is positive (since $t+1/t$ is decreasing on $(0,1]$ and increasing on $[1,\infty)$, and $t+1/t<s+1/s$ in between). The triangle area is half the fixed base $|A'B'|$ times this distance, so it is maximized exactly when $t + 1/t$ is minimal, i.e. (AM–GM) at $t = 1$. So $P' = (1,1)$.

**Conclusion.** The reflection $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$ preserves the hyperbola and areas, swaps $A'$ and $B'$, and fixes $P'$. It therefore maps the region between the hyperbola and chord $A'P'$ onto the region between the hyperbola and chord $P'B'$, so these two regions have equal area. Transporting back by $\phi_\lambda^{-1}$ gives the statement for $A, P, B$. ∎

putnam-2015-a1.title: Direct computation
putnam-2015-a1.body:
As above take $A=(t_1,1/t_1)$, $B=(t_2,1/t_2)$, $P = (t,1/t)$ with $0<t_1<t<t_2$.

**Maximizing the triangle.** The line $AB$ has slope $\frac{1/t_2-1/t_1}{t_2-t_1} = -\frac{1}{t_1t_2}$, i.e. it is $x + t_1t_2\,y = t_1+t_2$. The distance from $P$ to it is proportional to $t_1+t_2 - t - \frac{t_1t_2}{t}$ (positive between $A$ and $B$), so the area is maximal exactly when $t + \frac{t_1t_2}{t}$ is minimal, i.e. by AM–GM at $t = \sqrt{t_1t_2}$.

**Area cut off by a chord.** For $0<u<v$, the chord through $(u,1/u)$ and $(v,1/v)$ is $y = \frac{u+v-x}{uv}$ and lies above the (convex) hyperbola on $[u,v]$. The region between them has area
$$\int_u^v\left(\frac{u+v-x}{uv} - \frac1x\right)dx = \frac{(u+v)(v-u) - \tfrac12(v^2-u^2)}{uv} - \ln\frac vu = \frac{v}{2u} - \frac{u}{2v} - \ln\frac vu .$$
This depends only on the ratio $r = v/u$: it equals $F(r) = \frac12\left(r - \frac1r\right) - \ln r$.

**Comparison.** With $t=\sqrt{t_1t_2}$, the chords $AP$ and $PB$ have ratios $t/t_1 = \sqrt{t_2/t_1}$ and $t_2/t = \sqrt{t_2/t_1}$, which are equal. Hence both regions have area $F\big(\sqrt{t_2/t_1}\big)$. ∎

putnam-2015-a2.title: Closed form and divisibility
putnam-2015-a2.body:
The first terms are $a_0,\dots,a_5 = 1, 2, 7, 26, 97, 362$, and $362 = 2\cdot 181$ with $181$ prime (it is not divisible by $2,3,5,7,11,13$, and $17^2>181$). We show $a_5 \mid a_{2015}$.

**Closed form.** The characteristic equation $z^2 = 4z-1$ has roots $\alpha = 2+\sqrt3$, $\beta = 2-\sqrt3$, with $\alpha\beta = 1$. The sequence $\frac{\alpha^n+\beta^n}{2}$ satisfies the same recurrence and equals $1, 2$ for $n=0,1$, so $a_n = \frac{\alpha^n+\beta^n}2$ for all $n\ge0$.

**Divisibility.** Let $k$ be odd and $n\ge 0$. Since $k$ is odd, $x^k + y^k = (x+y)\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^j x^{k-1-j}y^j$, so
$$\frac{a_{kn}}{a_n} = \frac{\alpha^{kn}+\beta^{kn}}{\alpha^n+\beta^n} = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} (-1)^j \alpha^{(k-1-j)n}\beta^{jn}.$$
The right side is a sum of products of $\alpha=2+\sqrt3$ and $\beta=2-\sqrt3$, hence of the form $c + d\sqrt3$ with integers $c,d$. The left side is rational. Since $\sqrt 3$ is irrational, $d = 0$, so $a_{kn}/a_n = c$ is an integer: $a_n \mid a_{kn}$.

With $n = 5$, $k = 403$ (odd, $5\cdot 403 = 2015$) we get $362 \mid a_{2015}$, so $181 \mid a_{2015}$.

**Answer:** $181$ (one possible answer).

putnam-2015-a2.title: A congruence argument
putnam-2015-a2.body:
From the closed form $a_n = \frac{\alpha^n+\beta^n}{2}$ with $\alpha\beta=1$ we can also define $a_{-n} = a_n$ (as $\alpha^{-n} = \beta^n$), and we get the product formula
$$a_{m+j} + a_{m-j} = \frac{\alpha^m\alpha^j + \beta^m\beta^j + \alpha^m\beta^j + \beta^m\alpha^j}{2} = \frac{(\alpha^m+\beta^m)(\alpha^j+\beta^j)}{2} = 2a_ma_j .$$
Take $m = 5$ and work modulo $a_5 = 362$: then $a_{5+j} \equiv -a_{5-j}$ for every integer $j$. Putting $j = 5+k$ gives
$$a_{10+k} \equiv -a_{-k} = -a_k \pmod{362}.$$
Iterating, $a_{k + 10t} \equiv (-1)^t a_k$. Since $2015 = 5 + 10\cdot 201$, we get $a_{2015} \equiv -a_5 \equiv 0 \pmod{362}$. Hence $181 \mid a_{2015}$.

**Answer:** $181$.

putnam-2015-a3.title: Evaluate the inner product, then sum gcds
putnam-2015-a3.body:
**Claim.** For odd $n$ and any integer $a$, $\prod_{b=1}^{n}(1+e^{2\pi i ab/n}) = 2^{\gcd(a,n)}$.

*Proof.* Let $d = \gcd(a,n)$, $a = da_1$, $n = dn_1$ with $\gcd(a_1,n_1)=1$, and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n_1}$. Then $e^{2\pi i ab/n} = \omega^{a_1 b}$ depends only on $b \bmod n_1$, so the product over $b=1,\dots,n$ is the $d$-th power of the product over $b=1,\dots,n_1$. As $b$ runs over $1,\dots,n_1$, $a_1b$ runs over all residues mod $n_1$, so
$$\prod_{b=1}^{n_1}(1+\omega^{a_1b}) = \prod_{b=1}^{n_1}(1+\omega^b).$$
Since $z^{n_1}-1 = \prod_{b=1}^{n_1}(z-\omega^b)$, setting $z=-1$ gives $(-1)^{n_1}-1 = (-1)^{n_1}\prod(1+\omega^b)$; as $n_1$ is odd this is $-2 = -\prod(1+\omega^b)$, so the product is $2$. Hence the full product is $2^d$. $\square$

**Summing.** The double product is therefore $2^{\sum_{a=1}^{2015}\gcd(a,2015)}$, and the requested logarithm is
$$\sum_{a=1}^{2015}\gcd(a,2015) = \sum_{d\mid 2015} d\,\varphi(2015/d),$$
since exactly $\varphi(2015/d)$ values of $a\in[1,2015]$ have $\gcd(a,2015) = d$.

The function $F(n) = \sum_{d\mid n} d\,\varphi(n/d)$ is multiplicative (a Dirichlet convolution of the multiplicative functions $n$ and $\varphi$), and for a prime $p$, $F(p) = \varphi(p) + p = 2p-1$. With $2015 = 5\cdot13\cdot31$:
$$F(2015) = 9\cdot 25\cdot 61 = 13725.$$

**Answer:** $13725$

putnam-2015-a3.title: A shortcut for the key product
putnam-2015-a3.body:
Another way to see $\prod_{b=1}^{n_1}(1+\omega^b) = 2$ for odd $n_1$ ($\omega = e^{2\pi i/n_1}$): the factor $b=n_1$ is $1+1=2$, and for the others
$$\prod_{b=1}^{n_1-1}(1+\omega^b) = \frac{\prod_{b=1}^{n_1-1}(1-\omega^{2b})}{\prod_{b=1}^{n_1-1}(1-\omega^{b})} = 1,$$
because $2$ is invertible mod $n_1$, so $\omega^2,\omega^4,\dots,\omega^{2(n_1-1)}$ is a rearrangement of $\omega,\dots,\omega^{n_1-1}$ (and all factors $1-\omega^b$ are nonzero).

Then, as in the first solution, the exponent is $\sum_{a=1}^{2015}\gcd(a,2015)$. Counting directly with $p=5,q=13,r=31$: grouping by $d = \gcd(a,2015)$,
$$\sum_{d\mid pqr} d\,\varphi\!\left(\tfrac{pqr}{d}\right) = (p-1)(q-1)(r-1) + p(q-1)(r-1) + q(p-1)(r-1) + r(p-1)(q-1) + pq(r-1) + pr(q-1) + qr(p-1) + pqr,$$
which factors as $(2p-1)(2q-1)(2r-1) = 9\cdot25\cdot61 = 13725$.

**Answer:** $13725$

putnam-2015-a4.title: Compare with the set {1, 4, 7, ...}
putnam-2015-a4.body:
For a set $S$ of positive integers write $F(S) = \sum_{n\in S}2^{-n}$, so $f(x) = F(S_x)$. Let $T = \{1,4,7,10,\dots\}$; then $F(T) = \frac{1/2}{1-1/8} = \frac47$.

**Comparison lemma.** If $S\ne S'$ and the smallest element $m$ of the symmetric difference lies in $S$, then $F(S)\ge F(S')$. Indeed the two sets agree below $m$, $S$ gets $2^{-m}$ from $m$, and $S'$ gets at most $\sum_{n>m}2^{-n} = 2^{-m}$ from the numbers $\ge m$.

**Lower bound $f(x)\ge \frac47$.** Suppose $f(x) < \frac47 = F(T)$ for some $x\in[0,1)$. Then $S_x\neq T$, and by the lemma the smallest $m$ in the symmetric difference lies in $T\setminus S_x$. Now $\lfloor x\rfloor = 0$ is even, so $1\in S_x$, and $1\in T$; hence $m\ne 1$, so $m\ge4$ and $m\equiv 1\pmod 3$. Then $m-2, m-1\notin T$, and since $S_x$ agrees with $T$ below $m$, also $m-2,m-1\notin S_x$. So $\lfloor (m-2)x\rfloor$, $\lfloor (m-1)x\rfloor$, $\lfloor mx\rfloor$ are all odd.

Consecutive numbers among $(m-2)x, (m-1)x, mx$ differ by $x<1$, so each floor is either equal to the previous one or one larger; one larger would change the parity. Hence all three floors are equal, so $mx - (m-2)x = 2x < 1$, i.e. $x<\frac12$. But then $\lfloor 2x\rfloor = 0$ is even, so $1,2\in S_x$ and $f(x)\ge \frac12+\frac14 = \frac34 > \frac47$, a contradiction.

**No larger bound works.** Fix $n\ge1$ and let $x = \frac23-\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon<\frac1{9n}$. For $1\le k\le n$ we have $3k\varepsilon \le 3n\varepsilon<\frac13$, so
$$\lfloor (3k-2)x\rfloor = \left\lfloor 2k-2+\tfrac23-(3k-2)\varepsilon\right\rfloor = 2k-2,\quad \lfloor (3k-1)x\rfloor = \left\lfloor 2k-1+\tfrac13 - (3k-1)\varepsilon\right\rfloor = 2k-1,$$
$$\lfloor 3kx\rfloor = \lfloor 2k - 3k\varepsilon\rfloor = 2k-1.$$
So among $1,\dots,3n$ exactly the numbers $\equiv1\pmod3$ lie in $S_x$, and
$$f(x) \le \sum_{k=1}^n 2^{-(3k-2)} + \sum_{m>3n}2^{-m} = \sum_{k=1}^n 2^{-(3k-2)} + 2^{-3n} \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} \frac47 .$$
Thus for every $L'>\frac47$ some $x$ has $f(x)<L'$.

**Answer:** $L = \dfrac47$

putnam-2015-a5.title: Inclusion–exclusion modulo 2
putnam-2015-a5.body:
**Möbius count.** For $d\mid q$, the number of multiples of $d$ in $(0,q/4)$ is $\lfloor q/(4d)\rfloor$ (note $q/(4d)$ is not an integer since $q$ is odd). By inclusion–exclusion over the prime divisors of $q$,
$$N_q = \sum_{d\mid q}\mu(d)\left\lfloor\frac{q/d}{4}\right\rfloor \equiv \sum_{\substack{d\mid q\\ d \text{ squarefree}}}\left\lfloor\frac{q/d}{4}\right\rfloor \pmod 2,$$
since $\mu(d)=\pm1$ for squarefree $d$ and $0$ otherwise.

**Parity of $\lfloor m/4\rfloor$ for odd $m$.** Write $m = 8j + r$ with $r\in\{1,3,5,7\}$; then $\lfloor m/4\rfloor = 2j + \lfloor r/4\rfloor$, which is odd exactly when $r\in\{5,7\}$. Define $\chi(m) = 1$ if $m\equiv 5,7\pmod 8$ and $\chi(m)=0$ if $m\equiv1,3\pmod8$. Since $\{1,3\}$ is a subgroup of index $2$ of $(\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)^\times = \{1,3,5,7\}$, $\chi$ is a homomorphism to $\mathbb Z/2$: $\chi(mm') \equiv \chi(m)+\chi(m') \pmod 2$.

So $N_q \equiv \#\{d \mid q \text{ squarefree} : \chi(q/d) = 1\} \pmod 2$. Because every odd $d$ satisfies $d^2\equiv1\pmod 8$, $q/d \equiv qd \pmod 8$, hence $\chi(q/d) \equiv \chi(q) + \chi(d)$.

**Counting.** If $q = 1$, then $N_q = 0$ is even (and $q$ is not of the stated form). Otherwise let $p_1,\dots,p_r$ ($r\ge1$) be the distinct primes dividing $q$; the squarefree divisors are $d_I = \prod_{i\in I}p_i$ for $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,r\}$, and $\chi(q/d_I) \equiv \chi(q) + \sum_{i\in I}\chi(p_i)$.
- If $\chi(p_i) = 0$ for all $i$, all $2^r$ values are equal to $\chi(q)$, so the count is $0$ or $2^r$: even.
- If $\chi(p_j) = 1$ for some $j$, the involution $I\mapsto I\,\triangle\,\{j\}$ changes the value, so exactly half of the $2^r$ subsets have value $1$: the count is $2^{r-1}$, which is odd iff $r = 1$.

Thus $N_q$ is odd iff $r=1$ and $\chi(p_1)=1$, i.e. iff $q = p^k$ ($k\ge1$) with $p\equiv 5$ or $7\pmod 8$. ∎

putnam-2015-a5.title: Gauss-lemma style argument
putnam-2015-a5.body:
Let $S$ be the set of even numbers in $\{1,\dots,q-1\}$ coprime to $q$. The coprime residues come in pairs $\{a, q-a\}$ with exactly one even member, so $|S| = \varphi(q)/2$. Write $S = \{2a : 1\le a\le \tfrac{q-1}2, \gcd(a,q)=1\}$, so
$$\prod_{s\in S}s = 2^{\varphi(q)/2}\,R,\qquad R = \prod_{\substack{1\le a\le (q-1)/2\\ \gcd(a,q)=1}} a .$$
Reduce each $s\in S$ to the representative in $[-\tfrac{q-1}2,\tfrac{q-1}2]$. Distinct $2a, 2a'$ can never reduce to $\pm$ the same number (that would force $a\equiv \pm a'$, impossible in the range), so the absolute values of the representatives are exactly the $a\in[1,\frac{q-1}2]$ coprime to $q$. If $n$ elements of $S$ exceed $\frac{q-1}2$ (these get negative representatives), then $\prod_{s\in S} s \equiv (-1)^n R \pmod q$. As $R$ is invertible mod $q$: $(-1)^n \equiv 2^{\varphi(q)/2}\pmod q$.

The elements of $S$ below $q/2$ are $2a$ with $a<q/4$, so there are $N_q$ of them and $N_q + n = \varphi(q)/2$. Hence
$$(-1)^{N_q} \equiv (-1)^{\varphi(q)/2}\,2^{\varphi(q)/2} = (-2)^{\varphi(q)/2} \pmod q.$$
- $q=1$: $N_q=0$.
- $q$ has two distinct prime factors: the group $(\mathbb Z/q)^\times$ has exponent dividing $\varphi(q)/2$ (by CRT, its exponent is the lcm of the $\varphi(p_i^{e_i})$, all even), so $(-2)^{\varphi(q)/2}\equiv1$ and $N_q$ is even (as $q\ge 15>2$, $1\not\equiv -1$).
- $q = p^k$: $(\mathbb Z/q)^\times$ is cyclic of even order $\varphi(q)$, so $(-2)^{\varphi(q)/2} \equiv \pm1$ according to whether $-2$ is a square mod $q$, equivalently mod $p$. By the supplementary laws, $-2$ is a square mod $p$ iff $p\equiv1,3\pmod 8$. So $N_q$ is odd iff $p\equiv 5,7\pmod 8$. ∎

putnam-2015-a6.title: Reduce to the invertible case
putnam-2015-a6.body:
We prove the stronger identity
$$\det(A - tI - MX) = \det(B - tI - XM)\qquad\text{for all } t\in\mathbb R \text{ and all } X; \tag{$*$}$$
the problem is the case $t = 0$. Write $A_t = A-tI$, $B_t = B-tI$.

**Both sides are continuous.** Each side of $(*)$ is a polynomial in $t$ and the entries of $X$, hence continuous on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n\times n}$. The set $U$ of $(t,X)$ with $\det(A_t)\ne0$ and $\det X\neq 0$ is the complement of the zero set of the nonzero polynomial $\det(A-tI)\det X$, so $U$ is dense. Hence it suffices to prove $(*)$ for $(t,X)\in U$. Note $\det B_t = \det A_t$ (same characteristic polynomial), so $B_t$ is invertible too.

**Computation on $U$.** From $AM = MB$ we get $A_tM = AM - tM = MB - tM = MB_t$, so $M = A_tMB_t^{-1}$. Then
$$A_t - MX = A_t - A_tMB_t^{-1}X = A_t\,(I - MB_t^{-1}X).$$
Next, $(X^{-1}B_t - M)\,B_t^{-1}X = I - MB_t^{-1}X$. Taking determinants,
$$\det(A_t - MX) = \det A_t\cdot\det(X^{-1}B_t - M)\cdot\frac{\det X}{\det B_t} = \det X\cdot\det(X^{-1}B_t - M),$$
using $\det A_t = \det B_t$. Finally $\det X\cdot\det(X^{-1}B_t - M) = \det\big(X(X^{-1}B_t - M)\big) = \det(B_t - XM)$.

This proves $(*)$ on $U$, hence everywhere, and in particular $\det(A-MX) = \det(B-XM)$. ∎

putnam-2015-a6.title: Block decomposition
putnam-2015-a6.body:
Choose invertible $U,V$ with $U^{-1}MV = M' = \begin{pmatrix} I_r & 0\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ ($r = \operatorname{rank}M$). Put $A' = U^{-1}AU$, $B' = V^{-1}BV$, $X' = V^{-1}XU$. Then $A'M' = M'B'$ (multiply $AM = MB$ by $U^{-1}$ on the left and $V$ on the right), $A',B'$ have the characteristic polynomials of $A,B$, and
$$\det(A - MX) = \det(A' - M'X'),\qquad \det(B - XM) = \det(B' - X'M'),$$
since $U^{-1}(A-MX)U = A'-M'X'$ and $V^{-1}(B-XM)V = B'-X'M'$.

Write $A', B', X'$ in blocks of sizes $r$ and $n-r$. Then
$$A'M' = \begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&0\\A_{21}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M'B' = \begin{pmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}\\0&0\end{pmatrix},$$
so $A_{11}=B_{11}$ and $A_{21} = 0$, $B_{12}=0$. Thus $\chi_A = \chi_{A_{11}}\chi_{A_{22}}$ and $\chi_B = \chi_{B_{11}}\chi_{B_{22}}$; since $\chi_A = \chi_B$ and $A_{11}=B_{11}$, we get $\chi_{A_{22}} = \chi_{B_{22}}$ and in particular $\det A_{22} = \det B_{22}$ (the constant terms). Also $M'X' = \begin{pmatrix}X_{11}&X_{12}\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $X'M' = \begin{pmatrix}X_{11}&0\\X_{21}&0\end{pmatrix}$. Hence
$$\det(A'-M'X') = \det\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}-X_{11}&A_{12}-X_{12}\\0&A_{22}\end{pmatrix} = \det(A_{11}-X_{11})\det A_{22},$$
$$\det(B'-X'M') = \det\begin{pmatrix}B_{11}-X_{11}&0\\B_{21}-X_{21}&B_{22}\end{pmatrix} = \det(B_{11}-X_{11})\det B_{22},$$
and these are equal. ∎

putnam-2015-b1.title: Multiply by an exponential and use Rolle
putnam-2015-b1.body:
Let $g(x) = e^{x/2}f(x)$. It is three times differentiable, and differentiating repeatedly,
$$g' = e^{x/2}\left(\tfrac12 f + f'\right),\quad g'' = e^{x/2}\left(\tfrac14 f + f' + f''\right),\quad g''' = e^{x/2}\left(\tfrac18 f + \tfrac34 f' + \tfrac32 f'' + f'''\right) = \tfrac18e^{x/2}\left(f + 6f' + 12f'' + 8f'''\right).$$
(In operator form: $f+6f'+12f''+8f''' = (1+2D)^3 f$ and $e^{x/2}(1+2D)h = 2D(e^{x/2}h)$.)

$g$ has the same zeros as $f$, so at least five distinct zeros $x_1<\dots<x_5$. By Rolle's theorem, between consecutive zeros of a differentiable function there is a zero of its derivative, and these lie in disjoint open intervals, so they are distinct. Hence $g'$ has at least $4$ distinct zeros, $g''$ at least $3$, and $g'''$ at least $2$. Since $e^{x/2}\ne0$, the zeros of $g'''$ are zeros of $f + 6f' + 12f'' + 8f'''$, which therefore has at least two distinct real zeros. ∎

putnam-2015-b2.title: Each block of ten numbers loses exactly one sum
putnam-2015-b2.body:
Number the steps $0,1,2,\dots$ and let $s_n$ be the sum produced at step $n$ ($s_0 = 6$, $s_1 = 16$, $s_2 = 27$). Call $B_j = \{10j+1,\dots,10j+10\}$ the $j$-th block.

**Claim.** For every $j\ge0$: $s_j\in\{10j+5,10j+6,10j+7\}$; the summands used at steps $3j, 3j+1, 3j+2$ are exactly the nine numbers of $B_j\setminus\{s_j\}$; and
$$s_{3j} = 30j+6,\qquad s_{3j+1} = 30j+22-r_j,\qquad s_{3j+2} = 30j+27,\qquad\text{where } s_j = 10j+r_j .$$
Note the formulas say $s_{3j}\in B_{3j}$ at position $6$, $s_{3j+1}\in B_{3j+1}$ at position $22-r_j-10\in\{5,6,7\}$, and $s_{3j+2}\in B_{3j+2}$ at position $7$; so the first assertion for the indices $3j, 3j+1, 3j+2$ follows from the formulas.

*Case $j=0$* by direct computation: the steps are $(1,2,3;6)$, $(4,5,7;16)$, $(8,9,10;27)$; $s_0 = 6 = 10\cdot0+6$, and the formulas hold with $r_0 = 6$.

*Inductive step* for $j\ge1$, assuming the claim for all smaller indices. Before step $3j$, steps $0,\dots,3j-1$ have used as summands all of $B_0\cup\dots\cup B_{j-1}$ except the sums $s_0,\dots,s_{j-1}$, which were themselves crossed off. The other crossed-off numbers are the sums $s_k$ with $j\le k\le 3j-1$, and $s_k$ lies in block $B_k$ (this is known, since $k\le 3j-1$ is covered by the claims for indices $<j$). So before step $3j$: all numbers $\le 10j$ are gone, $B_j$ is missing only $s_j = 10j+r_j$ with $r_j\in\{5,6,7\}$ (here $j<3j$ is used), and blocks $B_k$ with $k\ge 3j$ are untouched.

- Step $3j$ takes $10j+1, 10j+2, 10j+3$ (as $r_j\ge5$); the sum $30j+6$ lies in the untouched block $B_{3j}$.
- Step $3j+1$ takes $10j+4$ and the two smallest of $\{10j+5,10j+6,10j+7\}\setminus\{s_j\}$, with sum $30j+4+(18-r_j) = 30j+22-r_j$; this lies in $B_{3j+1}$, still untouched.
- Step $3j+2$ takes $10j+8, 10j+9, 10j+10$, with sum $30j+27$ in the untouched block $B_{3j+2}$.

This proves the claim.

**Finding 2015.** If $m\equiv 2\pmod 3$, say $m = 3i+2$, then $s_m = 30i+27 = 10m+7$, so $r_m = 7$ and $s_{3m+1} = 30m+15$. We want $30m + 15\equiv 2015\pmod{10^4}$, i.e. $3m\equiv 200 \pmod{1000}$, i.e. $m\equiv 400\pmod{1000}$. Take $m = 1400\equiv 2\pmod 3$. Then
$$s_{4201} = 30\cdot1400 + 15 = 42015,$$
which ends in $2015$. (A finer analysis shows the first such term is $s_{1201} = 12015$.)

**Answer:** Yes — for example $42015$ is in the sequence.

putnam-2015-b3.title: Use the minimal polynomial
putnam-2015-b3.body:
Write the progression as $a = r-3s$, $b = r-s$, $c = r+s$, $d = r+3s$, so $M = rJ + sK$ with
$$J = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad K = \begin{pmatrix}-3&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}.$$
$S$ is the $2$-dimensional subspace spanned by $J$ and $K$.

**These work.** If $s = 0$: $J^2 = 2J$, so $M^2 = 2r^2J\in S$. If $r = 0$: $K^2 = 8I$, so $M^3 = s^3K^3 = 8s^3K\in S$.

**Nothing else works.** Suppose $rs\ne0$. Since $S$ is a subspace and $(-M)^k = \pm M^k$, replacing $M$ by $-M$ (i.e. $(r,s)$ by $(-r,-s)$) does not change the question, so assume $r>0$. We have $\operatorname{tr}M = 2r$ and
$$\det M = (r-3s)(r+3s) - (r-s)(r+s) = -8s^2,$$
so by Cayley–Hamilton $M^2 = 2rM + 8s^2I$. As $s\ne0$, $M$ is not a scalar matrix ($b\ne c$), so $I$ and $M$ are linearly independent and each power can be written uniquely as $M^k = t_kM + u_kI$. From $M^{k+1} = t_k(2rM+8s^2I) + u_kM$:
$$t_1 = 1,\ u_1 = 0,\qquad t_{k+1} = 2rt_k + u_k,\qquad u_{k+1} = 8s^2t_k.$$
By induction $t_k>0$ and $u_k\ge 0$ for all $k\ge1$, hence $u_k = 8s^2t_{k-1}>0$ for $k\ge2$.

Now $I\notin S$ ($1,0,0,1$ is not an arithmetic progression), $S$ is a subspace and $M\in S$, so $M^k = t_kM + u_kI\in S$ would force $u_kI\in S$, i.e. $u_k = 0$. This is impossible for $k\ge2$.

**Answer:** $M\in S$ has the property exactly when $a=b=c=d$, or when $M = s\begin{pmatrix}-3&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ for some real $s$ (i.e. $a+d = 0$).

putnam-2015-b4.title: Sum over a first
putnam-2015-b4.body:
For fixed positive integers $b,c$, a (nondegenerate) triangle with sides $a,b,c$ exists iff $|b-c|<a<b+c$. All terms are positive, so we may sum in any order:
$$S = \sum_{b,c\ge1}\frac{1}{3^b5^c}\sum_{a=|b-c|+1}^{b+c-1}2^a = \sum_{b,c\ge1}\frac{2^{b+c}-2^{|b-c|+1}}{3^b5^c}.$$
Split into $S_1$ ($b\le c$) and $S_2$ ($b>c$). For $b\le c$, $2^{b+c}-2^{c-b+1} = 2^c\left(2^b - 2^{1-b}\right)$, so
$$S_1 = \sum_{b\ge1}\left(\left(\tfrac23\right)^b - \tfrac{2}{6^b}\right)\sum_{c\ge b}\left(\tfrac25\right)^c = \sum_{b\ge1}\left(\left(\tfrac23\right)^b - \tfrac{2}{6^b}\right)\tfrac53\left(\tfrac25\right)^b = \sum_{b\ge1}\left(\tfrac53\left(\tfrac4{15}\right)^b - \tfrac{10}3\left(\tfrac1{15}\right)^b\right) = \tfrac53\cdot\tfrac4{11} - \tfrac{10}{3}\cdot\tfrac1{14} = \tfrac{85}{231}.$$
For $b>c$, $2^{b+c}-2^{b-c+1} = 2^b(2^c - 2^{1-c})$, so
$$S_2 = \sum_{c\ge1}\left(\left(\tfrac25\right)^c - \tfrac{2}{10^c}\right)\sum_{b\ge c+1}\left(\tfrac23\right)^b = \sum_{c\ge1}\left(\left(\tfrac25\right)^c - \tfrac{2}{10^c}\right)\cdot 3\left(\tfrac23\right)^{c+1} = \sum_{c\ge1}\left(2\left(\tfrac4{15}\right)^c - 4\left(\tfrac1{15}\right)^c\right) = \tfrac8{11} - \tfrac27 = \tfrac{34}{77}.$$
Hence $S = \frac{85}{231}+\frac{102}{231} = \frac{187}{231} = \frac{17}{21}$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac{17}{21}$

putnam-2015-b4.title: Ravi substitution
putnam-2015-b4.body:
Put $x = b+c-a$, $y = c+a-b$, $z = a+b-c$. Then $(a,b,c)\in T$ iff $x,y,z$ are positive integers, and they all have the same parity (pairwise sums $x+y = 2c$, etc., are even). Conversely, $a = \frac{y+z}2$, $b = \frac{z+x}2$, $c = \frac{x+y}2$.

*All even:* $x = 2u$, $y=2v$, $z=2w$ ($u,v,w\ge1$) give $a = v+w$, $b = u+w$, $c = u+v$, and the term $\frac{2^{v+w}}{3^{u+w}5^{u+v}} = \left(\tfrac1{15}\right)^u\left(\tfrac25\right)^v\left(\tfrac23\right)^w$.

*All odd:* $x = 2u-1$, etc. give $a = v+w-1$, $b = u+w-1$, $c = u+v-1$, and the term is $\frac{15}{2}$ times the same expression.

So
$$S = \left(1+\tfrac{15}2\right)\sum_{u\ge1}\left(\tfrac1{15}\right)^u\sum_{v\ge1}\left(\tfrac25\right)^v\sum_{w\ge1}\left(\tfrac23\right)^w = \tfrac{17}2\cdot\tfrac1{14}\cdot\tfrac23\cdot2 = \tfrac{17}{21}.$$

**Answer:** $\dfrac{17}{21}$

putnam-2015-b5.title: Hamiltonian paths and the position of 1
putnam-2015-b5.body:
Writing $\pi$ as the sequence $\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n)$, the condition says consecutive entries differ by at most $2$. So $P_n$ counts **directed** Hamiltonian paths in the graph $G_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $u\sim v$ iff $|u-v|\in\{1,2\}$. For $n\ge2$ each undirected Hamiltonian path has two directions, so $P_n = 2U_n$ where $U_n$ counts undirected ones. Note that $G_n$ restricted to $\{2,\dots,n\}$ is a copy of $G_{n-1}$ (shift by one).

Let $f(n)$ = number of Hamiltonian paths of $G_n$ starting at $1$, and $g(n)$ = number of undirected Hamiltonian paths in which $1$ is an interior vertex. Then $U_n = f(n)+g(n)$ for $n\ge2$.

**Paths from $1$ to $2$.** Let $h(n)$ count Hamiltonian paths from $1$ to $2$. $h(2) = h(3) = 1$ ($12$ and $132$). For $n\ge4$, the second vertex must be $3$ and the next-to-last must be $4$ (the neighbours of $1$ are $2,3$; those of $2$ are $1,3,4$), and deleting $1,2$ leaves a path from $3$ to $4$ through $\{3,\dots,n\}$; so $h(n) = h(n-2) = 1$.

**Recursion for $f$.** A path from $1$ continues with $2$ or $3$.
- $1,2,\dots$: the rest is a path in $\{2,\dots,n\}$ from its smallest element: $f(n-1)$ ways.
- $1,3,2,\dots$: then $2$'s only unused neighbour is $4$, so it is $1,3,2,4,\dots$ followed by a path in $\{4,\dots,n\}$ from $4$: $f(n-3)$ ways ($n\ge4$).
- $1,3,x,\dots$ with $x\ne2$: then $2$'s path-neighbours must come from $\{3,4\}$, and $3$ is already used up (its neighbours are $1$ and $x$), so $2$ is the last vertex. These are the paths from $1$ to $2$: exactly $h(n) = 1$.

So $f(n) = f(n-1)+f(n-3)+1$ for $n\ge4$, with $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=2$. Thus $c(m) := f(m+3)-f(m+2)-f(m) = 1$ for all $m\ge1$.

**Recursion for $g$.** If $1$ is interior, its path-neighbours are $2$ and $3$; replacing $2,1,3$ by the edge $2$–$3$ gives a Hamiltonian path of $\{2,\dots,n\}\cong G_{n-1}$ using the edge $\{2,3\}$, and this is a bijection. In $G_{n-1}$ (relabelled), paths using the edge $\{1,2\}$ are those where $1$ is interior ($g(n-1)$; they always use that edge) plus those starting $1,2,\dots$ ($f(n-2)$). So $g(n) = g(n-1)+f(n-2)$ for $n\ge3$.

**The combination.** For $n\ge1$,
$$f(n+5)-f(n+4)-f(n+3)+f(n) = c(n+2)-c(n) = 0.$$
For $g$, put $\Delta(m) = g(m+1)-g(m) = f(m-1)$ ($m\ge2$). For $n\ge2$,
$$g(n+5)-g(n+4)-g(n+3)+g(n) = \Delta(n+4) - \Delta(n+2)-\Delta(n+1)-\Delta(n) = f(n+3)-f(n+1)-f(n)-f(n-1) = c(n)+c(n-1) = 2.$$
Therefore for $n\ge2$,
$$P_{n+5}-P_{n+4}-P_{n+3}+P_n = 2(0+2) = 4.$$
(Check: $P_2,\dots,P_7 = 2,6,12,20,34,56$, and $56-34-20+2 = 4$.)

**Answer:** $4$

putnam-2015-b6.title: Regroup by the odd divisor, then integrate
putnam-2015-b6.body:
**Reindexing.** Write an odd divisor of $k$ as $d = 2\ell-1$ and $k = dm$. The condition $d<\sqrt{2k} = \sqrt{2dm}$ means $d<2m$, i.e. $\ell\le m$. Also $(-1)^{k-1} = (-1)^{m-1}$ since $d$ is odd. So the $k$-th term is $\sum \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{(2\ell-1)m}$ over the pairs $\ell\le m$ with $(2\ell-1)m = k$. (The series is not absolutely convergent, so regrouping needs care.)

Let $R(\ell) = \sum_{m\ge\ell}\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}$ (alternating series), with $|R(\ell)|\le\frac1\ell$, and set $S = \sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{R(\ell)}{2\ell-1}$, which converges absolutely. 

**Convergence to $S$.** The partial sum up to $N$ is
$$T_N = \sum_{\ell\in L_N}\frac1{2\ell-1}\sum_{m=\ell}^{\lfloor N/(2\ell-1)\rfloor}\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}m,\qquad L_N = \{\ell : \ell(2\ell-1)\le N\}.$$
So $T_N - \sum_{\ell\in L_N}\frac{R(\ell)}{2\ell-1} = -\sum_{\ell\in L_N}\frac{1}{2\ell-1}\sum_{m>\lfloor N/(2\ell-1)\rfloor}\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}m$. Each alternating tail is at most its first term $<\frac{2\ell-1}{N}$ in absolute value, so each summand is less than $\frac1N$. Since $\ell^2\le\ell(2\ell-1)\le N$, $|L_N|\le\sqrt N$, and the difference is at most $\frac1{\sqrt N}\to0$. As $L_N = \{1,\dots,\ell_N\}$ with $\ell_N\to\infty$, $T_N\to S$.

**Integral form of $R(\ell)$.** For $M\ge \ell$,
$$\sum_{m=\ell}^M(-1)^{m-1}\frac1m = \int_0^1\sum_{m=\ell}^M(-1)^{m-1}t^{m-1}dt = \int_0^1\frac{(-t)^{\ell-1}\left(1-(-t)^{M-\ell+1}\right)}{1+t}dt,$$
and the error term is at most $\int_0^1t^M dt = \frac1{M+1}\to0$. So $R(\ell) = \int_0^1\frac{(-t)^{\ell-1}}{1+t}dt$, and with $t = u^2$,
$$R(\ell) = 2\int_0^1\frac{(-1)^{\ell-1}u^{2\ell-1}}{1+u^2}du .$$

**Summing.** The series $\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{\ell-1}u^{2\ell-1}}{2\ell-1} = \arctan u$ converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ (alternating, tail after $L$ terms at most $\frac1{2L+1}$), so we may integrate termwise:
$$S = 2\int_0^1\frac{1}{1+u^2}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{\ell-1}u^{2\ell-1}}{2\ell-1}du = \int_0^1\frac{2\arctan u}{1+u^2}du = \Big[(\arctan u)^2\Big]_0^1 = \frac{\pi^2}{16}.$$

**Answer:** $\dfrac{\pi^2}{16}$
